title: Al-Barr, the Source of All Goodness
tomorrow: if you turn back late, does the door still open?

lines: POSTED HOURS, OR A QUIET FENCE?
cards: Some people post their volunteer hours. Some people fix the neighbor's fence and never mention it. Yesterday's question asked whether goodness is about facing the right way.

The Qur'an answers that one directly, in Pickthall's words: "It is not righteousness that ye turn your faces to the East and the West." So, one question for today: if it isn't the direction, what is it?

teach.b: The same verse keeps going. Righteous is the one who believes in God and the Last Day, and gives wealth, out of love for Him, to relatives, to orphans, to the needy, to the traveler, to those who ask.
Who prays, gives alms, keeps promises, stays patient in hard times.
The Arabic word for that righteousness is birr, and today's Name shares its letters: Al-Barr, the Source of All Goodness. Pickthall renders it the Benign: "Lo! He is the Benign, the Merciful."
Every good in the list flows from Him first.

teach.h: SPEND OF THAT WHICH YE LOVE.
teach.b: Another verse makes it personal: "Ye will not attain unto piety until ye spend of that which ye love." Not the leftovers.

Now a neighbor, the prophet Micah in the Hebrew Bible, answering the same question in his own words: "It hath been told thee, O man, what is good, and what the LORD doth require of thee: only to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God."
Here's what's shared, and it's worth saying out loud: both refuse to let goodness be a pose. Both send it into how you treat people. And here's an honest difference, ranking no one.
Micah sums it up in three strands: justice, mercy, humility. The Qur'an's verse begins with belief, then names, one by one, who should receive: the relative, the orphan, the stranger on the road.

how: Muslims give zakat, the required alms, and sadaqa, voluntary giving; 2:177 is recited as a summary of righteousness, and 3:92 is quoted about giving what you love.

o: the Pure, who has no fault in Him at all
the Rich, who owns every treasure there is
the Source of all goodness, the Benign

games.q: who says what about goodness — tap the pairs.
p: spend of that which ye love

s: in 2:177, righteousness means facing the right way to pray
the verse says it is not; it's belief lived out, giving to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler.
a verse says you won't reach piety until you give of what you love
"Ye will not attain unto piety until ye spend of that which ye love."
Micah and the Qur'an say exactly the same thing about goodness
they share a lot. Micah names justice, mercy, humility; 2:177 begins with belief, then names whom to give to.

games.q: your friend says, 'i pray every day, so i'm a good person, right?' what would 2:177 add?
o: prayer is in the verse, and so is giving to relatives, orphans, the needy and travelers.
yes; prayer settles it, and everything else is extra credit.
no; prayer doesn't count for goodness, only deeds for others do.
games.why: 2:177 puts belief, giving, prayer, alms and kept promises in one list. it refuses to make goodness a single thing.

practice: Bring to mind one person who could use some good from you this week: a ride, a meal, a few honest words about what they mean to you. Write that message now, or plan the act, and let the sit hold the person, not the credit.

wordCard.voice: Al-Barr. The Source of All Goodness, the Benign: the One every good deed in the list flows from.

orig.note: Arabic: the Source of All Goodness, the Benign. birr, goodness, is written with the same letters.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: goodness, aimed at a person, not at a direction. Name seventy-nine, given away.
